templates.name: Modifier placement: past participial opener (incl. Compared with that of)
Pronoun-antecedent agreement: possessive determiner its/their vs contractions
Subject-verb agreement, relative pronoun or possessive inside subject
Finite vs nonfinite, finite main verb
Plural vs possessive nouns: one- or two-slot spelling grid
Finite vs nonfinite, to-infinitive (purpose or after “the first”)
Finite vs nonfinite, finite second or subordinate verb

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (After + -ing), passage-final blank; the agent is the right subject
items.passage: The binturong, a tree-dwelling mammal of Southeast Asian forests, is known for an odor that many people compare to buttered popcorn. After analyzing urine samples from 33 binturongs living in captivity in North Carolina, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the smell was traced by researchers to a compound called 2-AP, which also forms when popcorn kernels are heated.
a compound called 2-AP, which also forms when popcorn kernels are heated, was identified by researchers as the smell’s source.
researchers traced the smell to a compound called 2-AP, which also forms when popcorn kernels are heated.
researchers’ conclusion was that the smell comes from a compound called 2-AP, which also forms when popcorn kernels are heated.
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes someone who analyzed urine samples from binturongs. Choice C places “researchers” immediately after the phrase, making clear that the researchers did the analyzing and then traced the smell to 2-AP.

A.recipe: passive that leaves the wrong noun as subject (V)
A.why_wrong: “The smell” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the smell analyzed the urine samples.

B.why_wrong: “A compound called 2-AP” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that a chemical compound analyzed the urine samples.

D.why_wrong: The subject is “conclusion,” not the researchers, so the sentence illogically says that a conclusion analyzed the urine samples.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (binturong odor traced to 2-AP, the compound behind the smell of popcorn; urine of captive binturongs in North Carolina; no researchers named). Band 6 as 188f7e3c (3.18) and d2b81427 (3.17): plain agent key after an After + gerund opener, passage-final options. Recipes V, W, P; the P foil opens with “researchers’,” the key's own noun, so the agent has to be the head, not a possessor. Each option read in the full sentence: only C leaves no dangling modifier.

band7.why: Plain agent key after an After + gerund opener, as band-6 models 188f7e3c and d2b81427; the possessive foil (researchers’ conclusion) is the only trap. Band 6 as targeted.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: past participial opener describing a thing acted on, passage-final blank
items.passage: Artists in Raghurajpur, a village in the eastern Indian state of Odisha, continue to produce pattachitra, intricately detailed paintings on cloth that traditionally depict episodes from Hindu mythology. Coated with a mixture of powdered chalk and tamarind seed adhesive and then repeatedly burnished with a smooth stone, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the cloth becomes a smooth, stiff surface ready for pigments made from minerals and plants.
artists make the cloth into a smooth, stiff surface ready for pigments made from minerals and plants.
the preparation of the cloth gives it a smooth, stiff surface ready for pigments made from minerals and plants.
pigments made from minerals and plants are then applied to the cloth’s smooth, stiff surface.
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes something that was coated with a mixture of chalk and adhesive and burnished with a stone. Choice A places “the cloth” right after the phrase, making clear that the cloth was coated and burnished before it became a surface for pigments.

B.why_wrong: “Artists” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the artists were coated with chalk and burnished with a stone.

C.why_wrong: The subject is “the preparation,” so the sentence illogically says that a preparation was coated with chalk and burnished.

D.why_wrong: “Pigments” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the pigments were coated with chalk and burnished with a stone.

items.notes: Subject: arts (pattachitra cloth painting of Raghurajpur, Odisha; the cloth is primed with chalk and tamarind gum and burnished with a stone before painting). Band 6 as 772835db and b369d54c: a past-participle opener describing a thing acted on, passage-final options. Recipes W (artists, a noun already in the passage), N, W (pigments). Key not the shortest option.

band7.why: Thing-acted-on subject after a past-participle opener, as band-6 models 772835db and b369d54c; the right subject is the obvious noun, not a property. Band 6 as targeted.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: noun-phrase appositive opener, passage-final blank; the right subject is the material, not the crater
items.passage: Images captured by NASA’s Dawn spacecraft in 2015 revealed unusually bright patches on the floor of Occator, an impact crater on the dwarf planet Ceres. A crust of salts deposited when briny liquid welled up from underground and evaporated, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Occator’s floor is partly covered by this bright material, mostly sodium carbonate.
Dawn’s images show that the bright material, mostly sodium carbonate, covers parts of the crater floor.
it is the bright material, mostly sodium carbonate, that covers parts of the crater floor.
the bright material on parts of the crater floor consists mostly of sodium carbonate.
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes a crust of salts. Choice D places “the bright material” right after the phrase, making clear that the bright material on the crater floor is the crust of salts left by the evaporating brine.

A.why_wrong: “Occator’s floor” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the crater floor is a crust of salts; the salts cover only parts of it.

B.why_wrong: “Dawn’s images” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the spacecraft’s images are a crust of salts.

C.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, leaving the phrase without a noun it can logically describe.

items.notes: Subject: natural science, astronomy (bright deposits in Occator crater on Ceres, imaged by Dawn in 2015, mostly sodium carbonate left by brine from below). Plan asked band 7, but R3_appositive has no band-7 official items (spec/rw/band7/form_structure_and_sense.md, section 5), so written as a strong band 6 with band_target 6, as w1b4_03 and w3b1_04 were. Move kept from band 7: the concrete nouns a student reaches for first (the crater floor, the spacecraft's images) are wrong; the right subject is the material itself. Recipes W, W, E; key not the shortest option.

band7.why: R3_appositive has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; strong band 6 (the concrete nouns a student reaches for first are wrong).

items.subtype: Possessive determiner before its antecedent (its vs their, possessive vs contraction)
items.passage: In 2009, chemists at Oregon State University investigating materials for electronics heated a mixture of yttrium, indium, and manganese oxides and were astonished when it turned a brilliant blue. Prized for ______ intense color, which, unlike that of many older blue pigments, resists fading even after prolonged exposure to heat, moisture, and sunlight, the pigment, named YInMn blue, is now commercially available for paints and plastics.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The blank refers to the pigment, which is named later in the sentence (“the pigment, named YInMn blue”). The singular possessive determiner “its” agrees with “the pigment” and shows that the intense color belongs to it.

A.why_wrong: “It’s” is the contraction for “it is” or “it has,” not a possessive determiner.

C.why_wrong: “They’re” is the contraction for “they are,” not a possessive determiner.

D.why_wrong: The plural “their” doesn’t agree in number with the singular noun it refers to, “the pigment.”

items.notes: Subject: natural science, chemistry (YInMn blue, found by accident in 2009 by Oregon State University chemists heating yttrium, indium and manganese oxides; now sold for paints and plastics). Band 7 as 0bcb4417: the determiner comes before its antecedent, “the pigment” 21 words later, with a plural noun of the other number between (“unlike that of many older blue pigments”) and more plurals a sentence back (chemists, oxides); options the 2 x 2 grid. Section 6: run 38 words, 35 after the blank, anchor outside the 6-word window. Famous topic kept: knowing it does not help choose its over their.

band7.why: Determiner 21 words before its antecedent, as 0bcb4417, with a plural noun of the other number between (“older blue pigments”) and plurals a sentence back; contractions are easy rejects, its vs their needs the whole run. Famous topic does not help: knowing YInMn blue tells nothing about its vs their.

fixes: explanation misquoted the passage (“called”); now quotes “the pigment, named YInMn blue”
hardened: added “unlike that of many older blue pigments” so a plural noun sits between the blank and “the pigment”

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement in a relative clause: plural antecedent before “that,” singular main subject and object
items.passage: Moonmilk, a white, pasty substance coating the walls of certain limestone caves, was once used in European folk remedies. Though it often consists of calcite, the mineral that also forms stalactites, moonmilk is composed of countless microscopic crystalline fibers that ______ it a consistency resembling that of cream cheese.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The blank is the verb of the clause beginning with “that,” which refers to the plural noun “fibers.” The plural verb “give” agrees with “fibers.”

B.why_wrong: “Gives” is singular, but “that” stands for the plural “fibers,” not for “moonmilk.”

C.why_wrong: “Is giving” is singular and doesn’t agree with “fibers.”

D.why_wrong: “Has given” is singular and doesn’t agree with “fibers.”

items.notes: Subject: natural science, geology (moonmilk, a soft cave deposit made of microscopic crystal fibers, once used as a folk remedy). Band 6 as ee4aa2aa: the blank is the verb of a relative clause whose antecedent, the plural “fibers,” sits just before “that,” while the clause's main subject (“moonmilk”) and the object after the blank (“it”) are singular. Wrong number in three tenses.

band7.why: Relative-clause verb with the plural antecedent right before “that” and singular moonmilk / it around it, the same setting as band-6 model ee4aa2aa. Band 6 as targeted.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: plural head behind a long relative clause full of singular nouns and verbs
items.passage: Fallstreak holes are circular gaps that occasionally appear in thin layers of cloud. The ice crystals that an airplane’s passage through such a layer, whose water remains liquid well below freezing, can trigger ______ rapidly by absorbing moisture from the surrounding droplets, eventually becoming heavy enough to descend and leave a hole in the cloud.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is the plural noun “crystals”; everything from “that an airplane’s passage” to “can trigger” describes the crystals. The plural verb “grow” agrees with “crystals.”

A.recipe: wrong number, present (agrees with the nearest nouns)
A.why_wrong: “Grows” is singular; it agrees with “passage” or “layer,” not with the subject, “crystals.”

B.why_wrong: “Has grown” is singular and doesn’t agree with “crystals.”

D.why_wrong: “Is growing” is singular and doesn’t agree with “crystals.”

items.notes: Subject: natural science, meteorology (fallstreak or hole-punch clouds: an aircraft crossing a layer of supercooled cloud sets off ice crystals that grow at the droplets' expense and fall). Band 7 as b32eab9f and 1c65db8f: plural head 18 words before the blank, behind four singular nouns (airplane, passage, layer, water) and a singular finite verb inside the intervener (“remains”); 21 run words follow the blank and none of them shows the subject's number. Section 6: run 43 words, attractors 4, intervener verb of the other number 1.

band7.why: Plural head 18 words before the blank behind four singular nouns and a singular intervener verb, nearest noun singular, 21 run words after the blank with no number cue; matches b32eab9f and 1c65db8f.

fixes: lightened the double center embedding (“which consists of water that remains liquid”) to “whose water remains liquid”; same attractors and intervener verb, easier to read

items.subtype: Past perfect for an action completed before a later past event (“when, in 1908”)
items.passage: The Tangut script, devised in 1036 for the Western Xia state, became unreadable within a few centuries of that kingdom’s collapse. Russian explorer Pyotr Kozlov ______ parts of Mongolia and Tibet on previous expeditions when, in 1908, he reached the ruins of Khara-Khoto, a Tangut city, and began excavating manuscripts written in the script.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence describes two past events: Kozlov’s exploring on previous expeditions and his arrival at Khara-Khoto in 1908. The past perfect “had already explored” shows that the exploring was completed before that later past event.

A.recipe: simple past where past perfect is needed
A.why_wrong: The simple past “already explored” doesn’t show that the exploring was finished before the 1908 arrival described in the “when” clause.

C.why_wrong: The present tense “already explores” doesn’t fit events that took place before 1908.

D.why_wrong: “Was already exploring” presents the exploring as going on at the moment he reached Khara-Khoto, but the text says it happened on previous expeditions.

items.notes: Subject: history (the Tangut script of the Western Xia, created 1036; Russian explorer Pyotr Kozlov reached Khara-Khoto in 1908 and began recovering Tangut texts). Plan asked band 7, but no R4 item in CB's bank sits above band 5 and the template has no band-7 officials, so written as a strong band 6 with band_target 6, modelled on 3.10 as w1b3_07 and w2b4_07 were: blank right after the subject, the deciding “when, in 1908” 9 words later, and 3.10's distractor set (simple past and past progressive with “already”, present). “On previous expeditions” rules out the progressive.

band7.why: R4 has no CB item above band 5, and model 3.10 is band 3 (filed hard). Cannot be band 6 or 7; kept as a hard-tier item in the shape of 3.10.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head behind an appositive holding a plural noun and its own plural verb
items.passage: Yakshagana, a form of theater from coastal Karnataka, India, combines dance, music, and improvised dialogue in costumed performances that often last all night. The bhagavata, a singer who narrates the story while two drummers keep the rhythm, ______ the pace of each scene.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is the singular noun “the bhagavata”; the phrase between the commas describes this singer. The singular verb “dictates” agrees with “bhagavata.”

A.why_wrong: “Dictate” is plural; it agrees with “drummers,” not with the subject, “the bhagavata.”

B.why_wrong: “Are dictating” is plural and doesn’t agree with “the bhagavata.”

C.why_wrong: “Have dictated” is plural and doesn’t agree with “the bhagavata.”

items.notes: Subject: arts, theater (Yakshagana of coastal Karnataka; the bhagavata sings the narration and leads the performance while chande and maddale drummers play). Medium as 2.20 and 2.22: singular head behind an appositive holding a plural noun with its own plural verb (“two drummers keep”).

fixes: options were set / are setting / have set / sets: “set” is also the simple past and fits a singular subject, a second grammatical option; verb changed to dictate (dictate, are dictating, have dictated, dictates)

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (Instead of + -ing), the agent is the right subject
items.passage: Osmanya, an alphabet devised in the early 1920s by Osman Yusuf Kenadid, was among several writing systems proposed for Somali, a language whose extensive literature had traditionally been transmitted orally. Instead of adopting Osmanya, however, ______ in 1972.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the Somali government made the Latin alphabet the official script for the language
the Latin alphabet was made the official script for the language by the Somali government
the Somali government’s choice for the language’s official script was the Latin alphabet
there was a decision by the Somali government to make the Latin alphabet official
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes someone who chose not to adopt Osmanya. Choice A places “the Somali government” right after the phrase, making clear that the government passed over Osmanya and made the Latin alphabet official instead.

B.recipe: passive that leaves the wrong noun as subject (V)
B.why_wrong: “The Latin alphabet” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the alphabet chose not to adopt Osmanya.

C.why_wrong: The subject is “choice,” not the government, so the sentence illogically says that a choice declined to adopt Osmanya.

D.why_wrong: The word “there” follows the phrase, leaving the phrase without a noun it can logically describe.

items.notes: Subject: social science, linguistics and language policy (Osmanya, the Somali script created by Osman Yusuf Kenadid around 1920 to 1922; in 1972 the Somali government adopted a Latin-based alphabet instead). Medium as 2.17 and 2.2: short preposition + gerund opener, agent key; recipes V, P, E.

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: object pronoun with a plural attractor just before it
items.passage: Published in 1938, Daniel Olorunfemi Fagunwa’s first novel was among the earliest book-length works of fiction written in the Yoruba language. In 1968, Nigerian playwright Wole Soyinka translated the novel, which follows a hunter’s adventures through a forest inhabited by supernatural creatures, into English, giving ______ the title The Forest of a Thousand Daemons.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun refers to the novel, which Soyinka gave an English title. The singular pronoun “it” agrees with the singular antecedent “the novel.”

A.why_wrong: The plural “them” doesn’t agree with the singular antecedent “the novel”; the nearby plural “creatures” is not what received the title.

B.why_wrong: The plural demonstrative “those” doesn’t agree with the singular antecedent “the novel.”

D.why_wrong: The pronoun “one” is unclear in this context; the resulting sentence doesn’t make clear what Soyinka gave the title to.

items.notes: Subject: literature (D. O. Fagunwa's 1938 Yoruba novel Ògbójú Ọdẹ nínú Igbó Irúnmọlẹ̀, translated by Wole Soyinka in 1968 as The Forest of a Thousand Daemons; the Yoruba title is left out so the antecedent is plainly “the novel”). Medium as 2.15: the plural attractor (“supernatural creatures”) sits just before the pronoun, inside a relative clause that interrupts the main clause.

fixes: option D “this” could be defended for a specific thing (CB 42cc9236 rationale); replaced with “one”, as in model 2.15

items.subtype: Simple past for a dated past action reported in a present-tense frame (“Historians note that ...”)
items.passage: In late 1872, Japan’s government suddenly replaced the country’s traditional lunisolar calendar with the Gregorian calendar. Historians note that officials ______ the change partly to save money: under the old calendar, 1873 would have had a thirteenth month, and government workers would have expected an extra month’s pay.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The change took place in late 1872, so the verb describing what officials did must be in the past tense. The simple past “timed” fits this completed past action.

A.recipe: present perfect for a dated past event
A.why_wrong: The present perfect “have timed” doesn’t fit an action completed at a specific past time, late 1872.

C.recipe: future for a dated past event
C.why_wrong: The future “will time” doesn’t fit an action that took place in 1872.

D.why_wrong: “Are timing” describes an action in progress now, not a decision made in 1872.

items.notes: Subject: history (Japan's switch from the lunisolar to the Gregorian calendar at the end of 1872, which spared the government a thirteenth month of salaries in 1873). Medium as 2.12: a dated past event in the first sentence, then “Historians note that officials ______”; foils present perfect, future and present progressive. The “would have” clauses are counterfactual and don't bear on the blank.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement in a relative clause: singular antecedent, plural nouns elsewhere
items.passage: Moist air flowing over a mountain range can oscillate in a series of atmospheric waves on the range’s downwind side. Near the crest of a wave, the air may cool sufficiently to produce a lenticular cloud, a smooth, lens-shaped formation that ______ stationary for hours even as powerful winds blow through it.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The blank is the verb of the clause beginning with “that,” which refers to the singular noun “formation” (the lenticular cloud). The singular verb “remains” agrees with “formation.”

A.why_wrong: “Remain” is plural, but “that” refers to the singular “formation,” not to “waves” or “winds.”

B.why_wrong: “Have remained” is plural and doesn’t agree with “formation.”

C.why_wrong: “Are remaining” is plural and doesn’t agree with “formation.”

items.notes: Subject: natural science, meteorology (lenticular clouds forming at the crests of lee waves downwind of mountains and staying in place while wind blows through them). Medium as 2.18: the blank is the verb of a relative clause; plural nouns elsewhere (“waves,” “winds”) are the attractors.

items.subtype: Simple present for a general fact
items.passage: Graupel, sometimes called soft hail, forms when a falling snowflake passes through a cloud of supercooled water droplets, which freeze onto its surface. Unlike genuine hailstones, which are dense and hard, graupel ______ easily when it is squeezed between two fingers, and it rarely causes the destruction associated with hailstorms.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The text describes what graupel generally does, using present-tense verbs such as “forms,” “are,” and “causes.” The simple present “crumbles” fits this general description.

B.recipe: simple past where the present is needed
B.why_wrong: “Crumbled” refers to a single past event, not to what graupel generally does.

C.recipe: past perfect where the present is needed
C.why_wrong: “Had crumbled” places the action before another past event, but the text states a general fact.

D.why_wrong: “Was crumbling” describes an action in progress in the past, not a general fact.

items.notes: Subject: natural science, meteorology (graupel, snow pellets formed when supercooled droplets freeze onto falling snowflakes; soft and easily crushed, unlike hail). Easy as 1.37 and 1.25: general-present frame with present verbs in both sentences.

items.subtype: Simple present for a habitual action (“Each spring”)
items.passage: In Kyrgyzstan, many herding families maintain a seasonal routine that is centuries old. Each spring, as snow melts in the surrounding mountains, these families ______ their livestock to high-altitude summer pastures known as jailoo, where they live in traditional yurts until autumn.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The phrase “Each spring” and the present-tense verbs “maintain,” “melts,” and “live” show that the text describes a repeated, current practice. The simple present “drive” fits.

A.recipe: simple past where the present is needed
A.why_wrong: “Drove” places the action in the past, but the text describes a yearly practice that continues today.

B.recipe: past perfect where the present is needed
B.why_wrong: “Had driven” places the action before another past event, which the text doesn’t describe.

D.why_wrong: “Were driving” describes an ongoing past action, not a repeated present one.

items.notes: Subject: social science, anthropology (Kyrgyz seasonal migration of herds to high summer pastures called jailoo, where families live in yurts). Easy as 1.17: “Each spring” plus present verbs before and after the blank.

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: object pronoun, singular antecedent
items.passage: Sous-verre, or reverse glass painting, has been particularly popular in Senegal since the early twentieth century. Because a sous-verre image is intended to be viewed through the glass on which it is painted, an artist must paint ______ in reverse order, beginning with intricate details and finishing with the background.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun refers to “a sous-verre image,” the thing the artist paints. The singular pronoun “it” agrees with this singular antecedent.

A.why_wrong: The plural “them” doesn’t agree with the singular antecedent “a sous-verre image.”

B.why_wrong: The plural “these” doesn’t agree with the singular antecedent “a sous-verre image.”

C.why_wrong: The plural “those” doesn’t agree with the singular antecedent “a sous-verre image.”

items.notes: Subject: arts (Senegalese sous-verre, reverse glass painting popular since the early twentieth century; details are painted first and the background last). Easy as 1.19 and 1.12: object pronoun, one singular antecedent in the same sentence, wrong-number demonstratives as foils.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, be-family options: singular head (a title) behind a short participial phrase
items.passage: In the early 1300s, Persian statesman Rashid al-Din served as chief minister to the Mongol rulers of Iran. His Compendium of Chronicles, completed around 1310, ______ one of the most ambitious early attempts to write a comprehensive history of the known world.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is the singular noun “Compendium” (the title of a single work), so the verb must be singular. The singular verb “is” agrees with it.

A.why_wrong: “Are” is plural; “Chronicles” is part of the title, not the head of the subject, “Compendium.”

C.why_wrong: “Have been” is plural and doesn’t agree with “Compendium.”

D.why_wrong: “Were” is plural and doesn’t agree with “Compendium.”

items.notes: Subject: history (Rashid al-Din, vizier of the Ilkhanate, and his Jami' al-tawarikh, the Compendium of Chronicles, completed about 1307 to 1310). Easy as 1.4 and 1.38: singular head with a short participial interrupter; the title's plural “Chronicles” is the only attractor.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, lexical verb: singular head behind a participial phrase
items.passage: Papakōlea Beach, located near the southern tip of Hawaii’s Big Island, ______ its distinctive olive-green color from olivine, a mineral that erodes from an old volcanic cone next to the shoreline. Because olivine crystals are comparatively dense, waves gradually carry lighter sand particles away while leaving the green crystals behind.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is the singular noun “Papakōlea Beach,” so the verb must be singular. The singular verb “gets” agrees with it.

B.why_wrong: “Get” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular subject “Papakōlea Beach.”

C.why_wrong: “Are getting” is plural and doesn’t agree with “Papakōlea Beach.”

D.why_wrong: “Have gotten” is plural and doesn’t agree with “Papakōlea Beach.”

items.notes: Subject: natural science, geology (Papakōlea green sand beach near South Point, Hawaii, colored by olivine eroded from a nearby cinder cone; the dense grains stay while lighter sand washes away). Easy as 1.20: singular head behind a participial phrase with no plural noun.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, lexical verb: named singular subject right before the blank
items.passage: Chilean writer María Luisa Bombal’s 1938 novel The Shrouded Woman (La amortajada) has an unusual narrator: Ana María, a woman who has just died. Lying in her coffin, Ana María ______ the relatives and former lovers who attend her funeral vigil, recalling her complicated relationship with each of them.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is “Ana María,” a single person, so the verb must be singular. The singular verb “observes” agrees with it.

A.why_wrong: “Observe” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular subject “Ana María.”

B.why_wrong: “Are observing” is plural and doesn’t agree with “Ana María.”

C.why_wrong: “Have observed” is plural and doesn’t agree with “Ana María.”

items.notes: Subject: literature (María Luisa Bombal's La amortajada, 1938, narrated by a woman lying dead at her own wake). Easy as 1.6: a named singular subject right before the blank, plural nouns only after it.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: missing main verb after a subject with an appositive
items.passage: Crushing a wintergreen-flavored hard candy in a darkened room produces a brief flash of bluish light. Methyl salicylate, the compound responsible for the candy’s flavor, ______ invisible ultraviolet light from the fracturing sugar crystals into visible light.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence needs a main verb for its subject, “Methyl salicylate.” The finite verb “converts” provides it and completes the sentence.

A.why_wrong: “Having converted” is not a finite verb, so the sentence has no main verb.

B.why_wrong: “Converting” is not a finite verb, so the sentence has no main verb.

D.why_wrong: “To convert” is not a finite verb, so the sentence has no main verb.

items.notes: Subject: natural science, chemistry and physics (triboluminescence of wintergreen candy: breaking sugar crystals give off ultraviolet light that methyl salicylate turns into visible blue light). Easy as 1.21 and 1.30: main verb after a subject with an appositive.

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive: singular possessor + plural noun, two-slot grid
items.passage: Babur, the founder of the Mughal Empire, composed his memoir, the Baburnama, in Chagatai, a Turkic language. Many of the ______ offer detailed descriptions of the vegetation, wildlife, and customs of India, which Babur frequently compared unfavorably with those of his homeland in Central Asia.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The passages belong to one memoir, so the singular possessive “memoir’s” is needed, and “passages” is a plain plural noun (“Many of the”), so it takes no apostrophe.

A.why_wrong: “Memoirs” lacks the apostrophe that shows the passages belong to the memoir.

C.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
C.why_wrong: “Passage’s” is possessive, but the noun here is simply plural.

D.why_wrong: “Memoirs’” is a plural possessive, but Babur wrote one memoir.

items.notes: Subject: literature, history (Babur's memoir, the Baburnama, written in Chagatai Turkic, with long descriptions of India's plants, animals and customs, often compared unfavorably with his Central Asian homeland). Easy as 1.16 and 1.36: possessor x plural grid; number cues “his memoir” and “Many of the.”

items.subtype: Past perfect for a state lasting up to a past point (“By the time ... died”)
items.passage: Eyak, a language historically spoken along the Copper River delta in southern Alaska, lost its last native speaker in 2008, after decades of documentation by linguists. By the time Marie Smith Jones died that year, she ______ the only remaining fluent speaker of Eyak for more than a decade.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The phrase “By the time Marie Smith Jones died that year” sets a point in the past, and the blank describes a situation that lasted up to that point. The past perfect “had been” shows this.

A.why_wrong: The present tense “is” doesn’t fit a situation that ended with her death in 2008.

B.why_wrong: The future “will be” doesn’t fit a situation that ended in 2008.

C.why_wrong: “Has been” describes a situation continuing to the present, but this one ended with her death in 2008.

items.notes: Subject: social science, linguistics (Eyak, Copper River delta, Alaska; Marie Smith Jones, its last native speaker, died in 2008, her sister having died in the mid-1990s). Easy as 1.24: an explicit earlier-than-past frame (“By the time ... died that year”); no simple past is offered, so no second defensible option.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: purpose infinitive after a complete clause
items.passage: Bermuda has no rivers or freshwater lakes, so its residents have long depended on rainfall for drinking water. Builders there traditionally give houses white, stepped limestone roofs ______ rainwater into storage tanks constructed beneath each building.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first part of the sentence (“Builders there traditionally give houses white, stepped limestone roofs”) is already a complete clause. The infinitive “to channel” begins a phrase that explains the purpose of the roofs.

B.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
B.why_wrong: “Channeled” adds a second main verb with no conjunction, making the sentence ungrammatical.

C.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
C.why_wrong: “Channels” adds a second main verb with no conjunction, making the sentence ungrammatical.

D.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
D.why_wrong: “Are channeling” adds a second main verb with no conjunction, making the sentence ungrammatical.

items.notes: Subject: engineering, architecture (Bermuda's white stepped limestone roofs channel rain into tanks beneath houses; the island has no rivers or lakes). Easy as 1.22 and 1.27: purpose infinitive after a complete clause; three finite foils only, so no -ing form can read as an acceptable participial phrase.

fixes: explanation quotes the clause in full instead of with an ellipsis

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: second verb of a compound predicate
items.passage: Drapo Vodou, the sequined flags displayed during Haitian Vodou ceremonies, often depict spirits or their symbols. To create one, an artist sketches a design on a piece of satin and ______ thousands of sequins and glass beads along its outlines, attaching them individually.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The blank follows “and,” so it holds the second verb of a compound predicate that begins “an artist sketches a design on a piece of satin.” The finite present-tense verb “sews” matches “sketches” and completes the sentence.

A.why_wrong: “To have sewn” is not a finite verb, so it can’t pair with “sketches” as a second main verb.

C.why_wrong: “Sewing” is not a finite verb, so it can’t pair with “sketches” as a second main verb.

D.why_wrong: “To sew” is not a finite verb, so it can’t pair with “sketches” as a second main verb.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Haitian drapo Vodou, sequined and beaded ceremonial flags on satin depicting spirits or their symbols). Easy as 1.11: second verb of a compound predicate after “and,” with 1.11's distractor set and the tense moved to the present.

fixes: explanation quotes the passage in full instead of with an ellipsis

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: -ing result phrase after a complete clause
items.passage: In 2009, a group of entrepreneurs in Sardinia, Italy, launched Sardex, a complementary currency that member businesses can spend only with one another. The participating firms buy goods and services from each other using Sardex credits rather than euros, ______ them to keep operating even when cash is scarce.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first part of the sentence is a complete clause, so the blank must begin a phrase that adds a result rather than a new clause. The participle “allowing” does this correctly.

A.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
A.why_wrong: “Allows” adds a second main verb with no subject or conjunction, making the sentence ungrammatical.

B.recipe: comma splice via pronoun + finite verb
B.why_wrong: “It allows” creates a second independent clause joined to the first with only a comma.

D.recipe: comma splice via pronoun + finite verb
D.why_wrong: “This will allow” creates a second independent clause joined to the first with only a comma.

items.notes: Subject: social science, economics (Sardex, a mutual-credit currency launched in Sardinia in 2009 that member businesses spend only with one another). Easy as 1.29: result phrase after a complete clause, two pronoun + finite comma-splice foils and one bare finite form.
